# Part X: Ecosystem and Economics {#part-ecosystem .unnumbered}

> "A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention."
>
> Herbert A. Simon, ["Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_economy)

By this point the reader has seen how models are trained, served, composed,
measured, and constrained. Part X asks who can afford to do those things, who
packages them for everyone else, and how the prices feed back into design. The
ecosystem is not scenery around the technical stack. It is one of the forces that
decides which parts of the stack become common practice.

@sec-model-landscape reads a model release as an economic and technical object:
weights or API, open or closed, capability or efficiency, license or lock-in.
@sec-tooling-ecosystem then follows the layers that grew around model calls,
tools, agents, gateways, observability, and authorization. @sec-economics gives
the cost structure underneath both: training and inference run on different
clocks, and the curves move in opposite directions as the field matures.

The reader should leave this part less impressed by any single leaderboard point
and more attentive to the terms under which capability is made available. A model
can be strong and still unavailable, cheap and still costly to operate, open and
still hard to use responsibly. Economics is where those differences become part
of the architecture.
